The Common side-blotched lizard (Uta stansburiana) is a small phrynosomatid that inhabits arid and semi-arid regions of western North America. Field surveys consistently report that even the largest individuals do not exceed 6 cm [Li = 6 cm] in snout-vent length, making this species one of the smaller members of its genus. Neonates emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a remarkably modest size, with a wet weight at birth of 0.35 g [Wwb = 0.35 g], a value that reflects the limited yolk reserves available during embryonic development. This diminutive starting mass imposes immediate constraints on juvenile foraging ecology and predation vulnerability, as hatchlings must begin exogenous feeding within days of emergence to sustain growth. Comparative data from related phrynosomatid species indicate that Uta stansburiana sits near the lower end of the body size spectrum for the genus, a trait that is likely linked to its relatively short generation time and high population turnover rates in unpredictable desert environments.

Sexual maturation in Uta stansburiana is tightly linked to body size rather than chronological age alone, a pattern common among small-bodied lizards. The snout-vent length at puberty for the population as a whole is 4.2 cm [Lp = 4.2 cm], though a notable sexual dimorphism exists in this threshold. Males typically require a slightly larger body size before reaching reproductive maturity, with the snout-vent length at puberty for males being 4.6 cm [Lp = 4.6 cm], a difference that likely reflects the energetic demands of male-male competition and territory defense. This divergence in maturation size between the sexes has been documented across multiple populations and is thought to be maintained by sexual selection on male body size, as larger males tend to secure superior territories with higher thermal quality and greater prey abundance. Juveniles that reach these size thresholds early in the active season are able to breed during their first year, while those born later may delay reproduction until the following spring.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions that simulate the warm summer temperatures typical of its active foraging period. When maintained at a constant temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], females achieve their maximum reproductive rate by producing an average of 4.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4.5 eggs per clutch] and depositing 3 clutches annually [F_R_i = 3 clutches annually]. This translates into a substantial seasonal investment in offspring production for an animal of such small body size. Multiple clutches are facilitated by rapid follicular development and a short interval between successive oviposition events, allowing females to allocate resources toward reproduction repeatedly across the breeding season. Gravid individuals show a noticeable increase in body mass prior to oviposition, and field observations confirm that females actively select nest sites with suitable thermal regimes to optimize incubation conditions for their eggs across the different clutches laid each year.

Incubation duration in Uta stansburiana is strongly temperature-dependent, a feature shared with many oviparous reptiles. Controlled laboratory experiments indicate that eggs incubated at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] require approximately 70 d [ab = approximately 70 d] to complete development and hatch, a relatively protracted incubation period that reflects the reduced metabolic rates of embryos at cooler temperatures. In natural settings, nest temperatures fluctuate considerably across the season and with depth, producing a range of reported incubation durations from 65 to 77 d at mean nest temperatures that are often unknown. Hatchlings emerging from extended incubation periods frequently exhibit larger body reserves and slightly greater mass, suggesting a potential trade-off between incubation duration and neonatal quality. This thermal sensitivity of embryonic development has important implications for population dynamics, as climate variation in the species' desert habitats can influence the timing of hatchling emergence and consequently the length of the growing season available to juveniles before winter dormancy.

Longevity records for Uta stansburiana suggest a relatively short lifespan compared to larger phrynosomatid lizards, a pattern consistent with its fast-paced life history strategy. The maximum lifespan recorded under field conditions at an ambient temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] is approximately 2325 d [am = approximately 2325 d], though most individuals in wild populations survive for only 1 to 2 years owing to high predation pressure and the physiological costs of repeated reproduction. This lifespan value emerges from mark-recapture studies that followed individuals from hatching through senescence, with the oldest documented animal persisting for approximately 2325 d. Age-related death in this species is typically preceded by a decline in body condition and a reduction in reproductive output during the final active season, consistent with patterns of reproductive senescence observed in other short-lived lizards. The combination of early maturation, high annual fecundity, and brief lifespan defines Uta stansburiana as a classic r-selected species adapted to the stochastic and resource-limited environments it inhabits.
